title: Synchronization: intrinsic monitors (object-level locks) prevent race conditions
shortTitle: How does synchronization work with intrinsic monitors?
keyPoints: Every Java object has an intrinsic monitor lock built into the object header's mark word.
synchronized acquires the monitor, guaranteeing mutual exclusion: only one thread in the critical section at a time.
The monitor also guarantees visibility: changes made inside a synchronized block are visible to the next thread that acquires the same lock.
The JVM optimizes monitors through biased locking, lightweight locking (CAS), and heavyweight locking (OS mutex).
Each monitor has an entry set (BLOCKED threads) and a wait set (threads that called wait()).
wait(), notify(), and notifyAll() must be called while holding the monitor lock, inside a synchronized block.

s1_definition.oneliner: Every Java object has an intrinsic monitor lock, and synchronized acquires it to provide mutual exclusion and memory visibility between threads.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Intrinsic monitor** – every Java object has a built-in monitor lock stored in the object header's mark word. You do not create it explicitly; it exists automatically.
- **Mutual exclusion** – when a thread enters a `synchronized` block, it acquires the monitor lock. No other thread can acquire the same lock until the first thread releases it.
- **Visibility (happens-before)** – all memory writes performed inside a synchronized block become visible to the next thread that acquires the same lock. This prevents stale reads.
- **Monitor sets** – each monitor has two sets: the entry set (BLOCKED threads waiting to acquire the lock) and the wait set (WAITING threads that called `wait()`).
- **Lock escalation** – the JVM optimizes monitors through three levels: biased locking (zero overhead for single-thread access), lightweight locking (CAS for low contention), and heavyweight locking (OS mutex for high contention).
s1_definition.analogy: Every object in Java comes with an invisible padlock. When you enter `synchronized(account)`, you grab the padlock. Only one person can hold the padlock at a time. Others who try to grab it must wait in line (entry set). When you release the padlock (exit the synchronized block), the next person in line grabs it. The padlock also guarantees that anything you wrote on the shared whiteboard inside the locked room is visible to the next person who enters.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Every Java object has an intrinsic monitor lock stored in the object header. When a thread enters a `synchronized` block, it acquires that monitor, guaranteeing mutual exclusion (only one thread in the critical section), visibility (writes are flushed to main memory), and effective atomicity (the critical section appears indivisible to other threads).

The JVM does not always pay the full cost of an OS mutex. It starts with biased locking (essentially free for single-thread access), escalates to lightweight locking (a CAS operation for low contention), and only falls back to heavyweight locking (OS mutex with thread parking) under high contention. Understanding this escalation helps explain why synchronization in low-contention code has near-zero overhead.

Remember one sentence: every Java object has a built-in monitor lock, and synchronized acquires it to provide mutual exclusion and memory visibility.
